overview: Kynance Cove is a small cove on the west side of the Lizard, about three kilometres north of Lizard Point. When the tide drops, white sand appears between islands and stacks of dark serpentine rock, a stone that’s rare in Britain and gives the cove its colours. It’s a gorgeous spot and it knows it, so expect company in summer.

Visitors have been coming since Victorian times, Queen Victoria and Prince Albert among them, and the National Trust now looks after the cove and the cliffs around it, which are protected for their plants and geology.

expect.title: Tides make the day
expect.text: Much of the sand and the paths between the rocks vanish at high tide, so check the tide times and aim for low water.

expect.title: The rocks
expect.text: Two kinds of serpentine meet here: the coarse, speckled stone you walk over on the way down, and the finer, banded stone of the islands and stacks.

expect.title: Café
expect.text: A café down in the cove has been serving visitors since 1929.

goodToKnow.label: Getting there
goodToKnow.text: No road goes to the beach: park in the National Trust car park on the clifftop and follow the footpath down. The coast path runs along the cliffs above.

goodToKnow.label: Busy times
goodToKnow.text: It’s small and fills up fast on summer days.

week.slot: Two hours to half a day
week.text: Plan your Lizard day around low tide at Kynance, then walk or drive on to Lizard Point, mainland Britain’s most southerly point. On a busy summer day, arrive early or late to find space on the sand.

pairWith.why: a bigger, wilder beach just along the coast

tips: Check the tide times before you go: low tide is when Kynance is at its most beautiful.
The walk down and back up is steep, so allow time and wear proper shoes.
